title: Peritoneal dialysis for chronic kidney disease
intro: Peritoneal dialysis is a form of kidney replacement treatment performed at home. A cleansing fluid is run into the abdomen through a soft tube, where the lining of the abdominal cavity filters waste and excess fluid from the blood. It offers flexibility compared with hospital haemodialysis, but requires careful hygiene and training.

sections.heading: How it works
paragraphs: A catheter, inserted in a minor operation, stays in the abdomen. Dialysis fluid containing sugar is run in, left for some hours, and drained with waste products and excess water drawn across the peritoneum. The process is repeated several times a day by hand, or overnight by a machine that exchanges the fluid automatically while you sleep.

sections.heading: Who it suits
paragraphs: It may suit people who prefer treatment at home, want to continue working or travelling, or live far from a dialysis centre. It requires the ability, or help from a carer, to perform exchanges in clean conditions. Previous abdominal surgery, severe hernias or very poor hygiene conditions may make it unsuitable.

sections.heading: Benefits and risks
paragraphs: Benefits include more independence, a gentler removal of fluid, and the ability to keep a more liberal diet and fluid intake than with haemodialysis for some people. The main risk is peritonitis, an infection of the abdominal cavity, which causes cloudy fluid, abdominal pain and fever and needs urgent treatment. Other problems include catheter problems, hernias, weight gain from the sugar in the fluid and, over years, loss of filtering ability of the membrane.

sections.heading: Daily life and care
paragraphs: Training lasts one to two weeks. Strict hand washing and a clean exchange routine prevent infection. Keep the catheter exit site clean and dry, and report redness, discharge or cloudy fluid at once. Regular clinic visits monitor blood tests and fluid balance. Diet advice usually involves protein, salt, potassium and phosphate. Many people can work, travel with supplies delivered abroad and maintain normal activities.
Transplantation, haemodialysis and conservative care are other options, and treatment may change over time.

sections.heading: Other kidney treatments
paragraphs: Peritoneal dialysis is one of several options. Kidney transplantation, haemodialysis in a centre or at home, and conservative care that focuses on symptoms are the others. Treatment may change over time, and the choice should reflect your health, your wishes and your home situation.

examples.title: Learning the routine
examples.text: Imagine you start training for overnight exchanges. You could ask the nurses to watch your technique, write down the steps and keep emergency numbers next to your supplies.

examples.title: Recognising a problem
examples.text: Suppose the drained fluid looks cloudy and you feel abdominal pain. You might call the dialysis unit immediately and bring the bag to the clinic.
